meta.description: The long-term profile of independent software developer Amiya_desi: GeoScore, Godot games, open-source tools, writing, and creative work.

letter.title: Hi, I'm Amiya_desi
letter.intro: This is not a resume, and not a live status feed. It is closer to a letter I rewrite every few months — for you, who happened to pass by this desk and want to know me a little better.

sections.heading: The name
paragraphs: I'm Amiya_desi, 19, a digital media technology student and an independent software developer. I build and maintain web software services, open-source tools, and Godot games. GeoScore is my main SaaS project today, while other unreleased software and games remain in development.

The name has no epic origin. Amia comes from Akiyama Mizuki, a character I used to love; desi comes from my bad hearing mishearing his catchphrase desu. When I learned programmer usernames only allow letters, digits and underscores, I joined the two with a _ — accidentally correct snake_case:
It's not proper Japanese at all, but after all this time, it has simply become me.

sections.heading: One rabbit hole after another
paragraphs: At 16, after climbing a flight of stairs, I suddenly decided to lose weight. No master plan, no supervision — just diet control, running and stair climbing, from a few laps to 3 km, 5 km, eventually 10 km. About 25 kg lighter in half a year. The process wasn't scientific, but it gave me my first transferable piece of self-evidence: I really can stick with something.

That experience is what I later used to convince myself to start making games. Undertale made me dream of indie games as a kid; in middle school I only dared to write settings in notebooks. At 17 I finally learned Python, installed Godot, followed tutorial projects, and stumbled into my first Game Jam.

Six jams so far. Some entries turned out fine, some failed hard — but the bottom line holds: every one of them got finished and submitted. After that it was one rabbit hole after another: AI for game dev, communities for resources, servers and domains from those communities, then articles and resource lists once the site was up, and lately even videos. The previous hole isn't filled yet, and my eyes are already on the next interesting one.

sections.heading: Things I've made
sections.intro: A few I'm willing to put on the table:

items.text: TimeRewindLinker: a puzzle game whose last 11 levels were ground out by AI plus my own brain — one of the few works I'll willingly reopen.
WakeUpAtTheBorder: a Godot 2D side-scrolling narrative game about a border, second prize at the 3rd GodotHub dev contest.
DelayTrace: a project I currently want to keep working on. I am leaving it here first and will add a fuller description later.
GeoScore: my main web software service, providing factual SEO / GEO audits, evidence maps, repair suggestions, and downloadable reports for public domains.

sections.heading: About AI
paragraphs: AI shows up in more and more of my workflow: writing code, digging up references, organizing notes, prototyping character setups and animation keyframes. Sometimes it's genuinely useful and rolls great ideas; sometimes it wrecks a project beyond recognition.

I don't want to introduce myself as an AI-tools account. AI is a tool I use — an amplifier, not the author. Real work still has to answer: did you build this with your own hands, trip over the pits yourself, and can you explain how it works?

sections.heading: Closing the letter
paragraphs: These days I love Sayori, Miku, 25-ji, Undertale and Re:0, and I still want to make a meta game that is truly my own. Those virtual worlds keep moving me — so I want to build a world that can move someone else.
I once asked AI to write a sentence for me, and I still like it: “I hope the data can fit me, and help me solve the things I can't figure out alone.”

So I'll keep writing, keep making, and keep leaving all this messy stuff on the internet. In a few months this letter will probably be rewritten — by then there should be new bonds, and a bit more skill.

signature.ps: P.S. If anything in this letter resonates, feel free to leave a small note on the guestbook.

items.question: What is sayori.org?
items.answer: It is the personal site of independent software developer Amiya_desi, presenting GeoScore, Godot games, open-source tools, writing, public projects, and contact details.

items.question: What does the blog cover?
items.answer: blog.sayori.org mainly records tutorials, server tinkering, Godot development, AI tools and student resources, mobile privacy, resource indexes, project logs and everyday echoes.

items.question: What products are you developing?
items.answer: My current focus is web software such as GeoScore, alongside Godot games, desktop and developer tools, and open-source software. GeoScore is currently free to use, and this site does not yet offer paid subscriptions or checkout. Prices, delivery, refund, and cancellation terms will be published before any paid plan or software sale launches.

items.question: How can I reach you or learn more?
items.answer: Email me@sayori.org, or continue from here to GitHub, the blog, Bilibili, itch.io, YouTube, Linux.do and the guestbook.
